Typically, the amount of decay heat that will be present in the reactor immediately following shutdown will be roughly 7% of the power level that the reactor operated at prior to shutdown.
Decay heat may decrease to about 2% of the pre-shutdown power level within the first hour after shutdown and to 1% within the first day.

summary.text: Heat is energy transferred as a result of a temperature difference. Temperature is a measure of the molecular energy in a substance.
Heat flux is the rate of heat transfer per unit area.
Fourier's Law of Conduction solves rectangular and cylindrical problems, and conduction problems can use electrical analogies.
When conduction and convection both occur, the overall heat transfer coefficient must be used.
Counter-flow heat exchangers typically remove more heat than parallel flow heat exchangers.
Regenerative heat exchangers return energy to the system. Non-regenerative heat exchangers reject heat to the surroundings.
The thermal power of a reactor is directly related to coolant mass flow rate and the temperature difference across the core.
Decay heat depends on the reactor's power history, and methods for removing it are closed loop or once through.

p.44 and p.51 say heat generation is proportional to the thermal neutron flux. The lesson uses the wording on p.45, which says the neutron flux.
The handbook's 7% decay heat value is used by the user's decision, Nov 5, 2026. Thermal Hydraulics.docx slide 1.27 says approximately 6%, and that value is not shown.

p.50 says heat crosses the helium gap of oxide fuel by convection. Heat Transfer.docx slides 1.15 and 1.23 say conduction. Neither is used, since the gap in this reactor is liquid sodium (Thermal Hydraulics.docx slide 1.10). Existing item Q304 teaches conduction and should be reviewed.

Fuel changes on p.50 and p.51 (zircaloy, oxide pellets, clad creep, crud) describe other reactors. The 3400 MW example has no water content and is kept for objective 2.4.
